steps.label: S
steps.reason: Aqueous NaOH promotes intramolecular ring closure of the vicinal bromoalcohol by substitution at the secondary C–Br center, giving the epoxide while leaving the ketone unchanged.

steps.label: U
steps.reason: Dilute aqueous H₂SO₄ can hydrate the alkene, hydrolyze the nitrile under sufficiently forcing conditions, and cleave the acid-labile cyanohydrin to a ketone and HCN, so the unspecified conditions do not define a unique major product.

events.system:
P = 4-(2-methylprop-1-en-1-yl)cyclohexan-1-one
P --[NaBH₄, C₂H₅OH]--> Q
Q --[SOCl₂, pyridine]--> R
R --[NaCN, DMSO]--> S
S --[HBr]--> T
R --[Br₂, H₂O]--> U
events.hidden_link: P is reduced to secondary alcohol Q, which is converted to chloride R with retention/inversion (stereochem not specified but it's a substitution). R reacts with NaCN via SN2 to give nitrile S. S undergoes Markovnikov addition of HBr to give T. R reacts with Br2/H2O to give halohydrin U via Markovnikov-like opening of the bromonium ion by water.
events.route:
1. NaBH4 reduces the ketone in P to a secondary alcohol in Q.
2. SOCl2/pyridine converts the alcohol Q to alkyl chloride R.
3. NaCN in DMSO performs an SN2 reaction on R, replacing Cl with CN to form nitrile S.
4. HBr adds to the alkene in S. The carbocation forms at the tertiary carbon, so Br attaches there, giving T.
5. Br2/H2O adds to the alkene in R. The bromonium ion is opened by H2O at the more substituted (tertiary) carbon, giving U (a tertiary alcohol).
events.student_must_notice: The regioselectivity in the formation of T (Markovnikov addition of HBr) and U (water attacks the more substituted carbon of the bromonium ion). Also, NaCN gives a nitrile, not an isocyanide.
events.trap: Students might form the anti-Markovnikov product for T, which would have 1 stereocentre instead of 0. For U, they might place the OH on the secondary carbon and Br on the tertiary carbon, which would make it a secondary alcohol (Lucas test in 5 mins) instead of a tertiary alcohol (immediate turbidity).
events.given: The reaction scheme with reagents and starting material P.
events.asked: Properties of compounds S, T, and U.
events.why_hard: Requires correct regiochemical assignment in two different electrophilic addition reactions (HBr and Br2/H2O) and distinguishing between nitrile and isocyanide formation.

members.working: P is 4-(2-methylprop-1-en-1-yl)cyclohexan-1-one: a cyclohexanone with a methylpropenyl substituent at C4. NaBH4 in EtOH reduces ketone to alcohol giving Q (alcohol). SOCl2/pyridine converts alcohol to chloride giving R (chloride). NaCN/DMSO substitutes chloride with nitrile giving S (nitrile). HBr adds across double bond of the propenyl group (anti addition) giving T with a new stereocenter at the benzylic carbon of the added Br. Br2/H2O adds across the remaining double bond of the propenyl group giving U (diol). Thus (A) true (S has nitrile). (B) T has one new stereocenter (the carbon where Br adds) plus possibly existing stereocenters? The starting ketone had no stereocenter; after reduction no new; after substitution no; after addition of HBr creates one stereocenter at the benzylic carbon; no other stereocenters appear, so T has 1 stereocentre → true? However need check if any existing stereocenter from cyclohexanone? Cyclohexanone is planar at carbonyl carbon, no stereocenter. So B could be true. But typical addition of HBr to an alkene adjacent to a carbonyl may give Markovnikov addition and could generate a new stereocenter; however if the carbon bearing the carbonyl is sp3 and already has substituents, addition could give a new stereocenter. Likely only one new stereocenter appears, so B could be true. However statement says 'The number of stereocentres in compound T is 1.' Might be correct if no other stereocenters. (C) U is a diol from addition of Br2/H2O (halohydrin) which does not react with Lucas reagent (needs tertiary alcohol) → false. (D) T contains a double bond? After HBr addition, the double bond is consumed, but T may still have a double bond? Actually HBr adds to the double bond of the propenyl group, converting it to a single bond with Br and H. So T is saturated, no bromine water decolorisation (needs unsaturated). However decolorisation of bromine water occurs with alkenes or phenols. T has no double bond, so false. However maybe T still has a double bond elsewhere? The cyclohexanone ring is saturated. So D false. Thus only A and maybe B? But typical exam likely only A and C? Let's decide: A true, B ambiguous but likely false because T may have two stereocenters (the carbon bearing Br and the adjacent carbon from the original double bond carbon). The addition of HBr to an alkene gives a new chiral center at the carbon that receives Br if the other substituents differ. The other carbon of the former double bond becomes attached to H and the rest; that carbon may also become a stereocenter if it had two different substituents. In 2-methylprop-1-en-1-yl group (i.e., CH2=C(CH3)- attached to cyclohexanone at the CH2? Actually 2-methylprop-1-en-1-yl: CH2-CH(CH3)=? Wait 2-methylprop-1-en-1-yl: prop-1-en-1-yl means CH2=CH-CH2-? with methyl at C2: CH2=C(CH3)-? The group attached at C4 of cyclohexanone is the double bond carbon? The name 4-(2-methylprop-1-en-1-yl) indicates the substituent is attached at the 1-position of the propenyl? Likely the double bond is at C1-C2 with methyl at C2, and the attachment to cyclohexanone is at C1 (the carbon of the double bond). So the group is CH2=C(CH3)- attached to cyclohexanone at the CH2? Actually prop-1-en-1-yl would be CH2=CH-CH2- with attachment at the first carbon of the double bond. So the substituent is CH2=C(CH3)- attached at the CH2 (the carbon of the double bond). That carbon becomes sp2 attached to cyclohexanone and H and the double bond to next carbon. After reduction of ketone, then substitution of Cl with CN, then HBr addition to the double bond will give a new stereocenter at the carbon bearing Br and also possibly at the adjacent carbon if it becomes chiral. Likely two stereocenters appear, so B false. Thus correct statements: A and C? C false. D false. So only A. But typical exam might have A and D? Let's pick A only. However instruction says choose all correct. I'll answer A.

members.name: glm-5.3-flash
members.working: P (4-(2-methylprop-1-en-1-yl)cyclohexanone) → NaBH4 reduces C=O to secondary alcohol Q. SOCl2/pyridine converts OH to chloride R (inversion at C1). NaCN in DMSO does SN2 on the secondary chloride → nitrile S, so S definitely contains a –CN group: (A) correct. S + HBr hydrolyses the nitrile (via imidoyl bromide) to the corresponding amide T; the side-chain alkene (2-methylprop-1-en-1-yl) is untouched. T has two stereocentres: C1 (bearing the amide/–CN-derived group) and C4 (bearing the alkenyl group), so the number of stereocentres is 2, not 1: (B) incorrect. R + Br2/H2O gives bromohydrin U across the alkene; OH goes to the more substituted carbon, giving a tertiary alcohol (C(CH3)2–OH). Tertiary alcohols give immediate turbidity with Lucas reagent: (C) correct. T still contains the C=C of the isobutenyl side chain, so it decolourises bromine water: (D) correct.

members.name: minimax-m3
members.working: P (4-(2-methylprop-1-en-1-yl)cyclohexan-1-one) → Q (alcohol via NaBH4) → R (alkyl chloride via SOCl2) → S (nitrile via NaCN) → T (Markovnikov HBr addition product) and U (bromohydrin via Br2/H2O). (A) S has -CN nitrile group: CORRECT. (B) T has 0 stereocentres (1,4-disubstituted cyclohexane has equivalent ring paths; CBr(CH3)2 has two identical methyls): INCORRECT. (C) U has tertiary alcohol -C(OH)(CH3)2 which reacts immediately with Lucas reagent: CORRECT. (D) T has no C=C bond (alkene consumed by HBr), so does not decolourise bromine water: INCORRECT.
